Question of the Day #235: If you could travel to one of the planets, which planet would you go to?

posts.name: Ronway
posts.cooked: Uranus.

If it has to be the planet as it actually exists (but I can magically survive the conditions there), I’d probably pick Pluto (it’s a planet shut up). The idea of being so far away that the sun is just another star appeals greatly to my preference for darkness; I’d enjoy it on the same level that I enjoy walking around on a winter’s night, if it’s not too cold to be unbearable, and I get to sightsee by starlight and enjoy my solitude.

But what I really want to do is travel to the version of the planet Venus that existed in pulp-era novels, before our space program figured out that it was just a ball of high-pressure acid. The literary Venus, as described in novels such as Otis Kline’s “Planet of Peril”, is a sweltering jungle world surrounded by constant clouds of white fog (but normal clouds that are limited to the atmosphere, not clouds of acid that stretch as far as the ground). Even if it wasn’t also a planet of space babes (ranging from barbaric Amazons to damseled princesses), if it was just a wilderness of cypress swamps and dinosaurs and palm trees and warring desert tribes, and I could be some sort of John Carter type of hero adventuring across such an environment, that would be awesome.

posts.cooked: Namek.
I also would really enjoy Nibiru, particularly the one in Star Trek Into Darkness. A totally red forest? Yes please!

Pluto (it’s a planet shut up)

Woo hoo! Pluto-Believer High-Five!

Otherwise . . . let’s go with Pluto, just to Spite those that doubt its planet-ness.

Question of the Day #236: You can only have the SotM Core Set and one expansion. Which one do you choose? We’re assuming EE, for obvious reasons. Rook City, Infernal Relics, Shattered Timelines, and Wrath of the Cosmos sold separately. The Mini-expansions and variants are included in the set they were originally released with.

Infernal Relics. Nightmist is one of my three favorite heroes, Argent is also fun, and three of the four villains are in my top ten. The environments kinda suck, but you can’t have everything. Vengeance and OblivAeon give you more heroes to choose from, and the latter is really tempting because it also contains five environments, but if you only have the core set plus OblivAeon, you’re going to get really tired of fighting the same four villains over and over (I should know, I did exactly this after purchasing the app last year). The Big O doesn’t actually hit the table often enough to be a good investment, and the same is true to a lesser extent with the V5 (plus only two Environments…if it had three more then we’d be at an even 30, and then I might consider it in order to get Natch and the Sentinels). Wrath of the Cosmos is the only other one that’s even tempting; RC is just kind of awful as a set, with only three really good decks in it, and Shattered Timelines has two excellent heroes but only two villains that aren’t hair-tearing-out levels of unpleasant to go up against. (And VOTM has no heroes at all, so even though it gives you lots of variety in opponents, I can’t even consider it.)

My Reply to QotD #236: (Disclaimer: I pretty much like all the decks almost equally; I’m only trying to find faults in them for the purpose of elimination.) Villains of the Multiverse has no Heroes, so no. And Vengeance has no single-Deck Villains, so also no. The Organisation, The Matriarch, and Rook City are all pretty tough, and Mister Fixer, Expatriette, and Spite aren’t the most balanced/fun decks, so let’s say no to Rook City. I like NightMist and AA, but they are very complex, and Apostate is kinda a drag, so I’ll cross off Infernal Relics. OblivAeon is very tempting, with five Heroes and Environments each . . . but the Villain itself doesn’t have much mileage. Let’s see, of the remaining two sets (WotC & ST), I think I can’t find any preferences regarding any of the Heroes or Environments. Regarding Villains, each set has one very tough opponent (Progeny and IL) . . . erm, I guess I’ll go with Shattered Timelines, as (for me, at least) the Villains in Wrath of the Cosmos are, on average, more difficult. Mind you, this isn’t me say that Shattered Timelines is “the best set,” or any such thing. I don’t really think that there’s one set that’s completely better than all the others.

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
Halfling. Especially after seeing Runesmith’s video on them.

They are basically born retired. Can’t beat that.

There are several more obscure races that premiered after D&D was bought by Wizards of the Coast, which I find far more interesting than the standard Tolkien knock-offs of original D&D, or even the handful of 2E creations such as tieflings or Thri-Kreen, all of which are describable in a sentence or two. I’m going to give three possible choices, depending on just how indulgent the “Dungeon Master” is when transforming me into one of them (a la the D&D cartoon).

#3 - Shardmind. I don’t actually know the details of this species, as they came from the 4th Edition, which I never played. But they’re some sort of inorganic living crystal creature with natural psionic abilities, so I’m automatically interested. Even if their innate abilities are useless, just not having to eat or perhaps even breathe would be reason enough for me to enjoy being one of them.

#2 - Spellscale. From Races of the Dragon, this species of natural sorcerers have thin dragon-like scales but are still pretty human-looking, which is “best of both worlds” stuff from my perspective. However, one of their main racial abilities is that they can pray to a different one of the dragon deities every day, gaining special powers particular to that god’s particular portfolio. I wouldn’t want to be a spellscale if these deities didn’t actually exist, at least enough that meditating on their concept wouldn’t grant the powers involved. And given that I myself have always ruled that dragons shouldn’t HAVE gods, whenever I’m the DM, it would be highly surprising if I found myself able to draw power from such entities.

#1 - Changeling. From the Eberron campaign setting. No powerset is of greater interest to me than shape-shifting, and these half-doppelgangers can automatically change their appearance completely, with all the indications being that it’s not a merely skin-deep pretense, but a complete bodily transformation that will fool even the closest inspection. The ability to reinvent my identity on the fly would be astonishingly useful, particularly given my lack of social graces; every time some disastrous faux pas destroys all my existing friendships, I can take on a new persona and either win back those allies or find new ones. Literally no single superpower would be as useful to me as this (unless “omnipotence” is an option).

The_Justifier:

The ability to reinvent my identity on the fly would be astonishingly useful, particularly given my lack of social graces; every time some disastrous faux pas destroys all my existing friendships, I can take on a new persona and either win back those allies or find new ones.

Sure, but if you’re a changeling in our world, there’s the matter of social security numbers, driver’s licenses, bank accounts, etc. (Of course, the QotD did kinda leave it ambiguous whether one would remain in our world or be moved to a fantasy world.)

My Reply to QotD #240: Hmm . . . Gnomes are quite a bit smarter, on average, than humans, so I might enjoy being one of them. Having the psionic powers of a Gith could be fun. Of course, Elves are pretty much better than everyone else at pretty much everything, so there’s that. And I’d also definitely want to jump on the halfling bandwagon.
